Those shard jobs on PR #371 aren't anything the PR added — they're the repo's standing Windows CI sharding harness (`tools/ci-bench/windows-production`, wired into `.github/workflows/test.yml`).

**Why they exist**

- The `internal/cli` suite runs on Windows under the Go race detector with atomic coverage (`go test -race -covermode=atomic -coverpkg=./...`). That combination on Windows runners is far too slow for one job — each shard already gets a 35-minute timeout.
- So CI compiles the test binary once, inventories every Test/Example/Fuzz root, and partitions them across 8 parallel ephemeral Windows runners (`windows-test-shards` matrix), balanced by historical timing weights. Everything else on Windows runs once in a separate non-heavy job.
- A verifier job then proves no test was silently dropped: exact root coverage, no duplicates or omissions, race-instrumentation evidence, and it unions the per-shard coverage profiles into one report — which is why there's no separate full-suite Windows coverage job.
- The whole thing collapses back into the single required check name `test (windows-latest)`, which fails if any prepare/shard/vet/verify job fails.
- It was ported from entire-graph PR #189 (`tools/ci-bench/windows-production/README.md` records the source revision), introduced in commits `6a20d16a` and `dee58bc9`.

Shard runtimes from yesterday's green run on `main`-adjacent CI:

- 8 shards at 3–7 minutes each (~34 minutes of total Windows test execution), plus 2m compile/plan, 2m non-heavy packages, 1m vet.
- Critical path with sharding: ~10 minutes wall clock. macOS runs the same suite unsharded in 20m, Ubuntu in 11m.

**What it's for:** running the full `internal/cli` suite under the Go race detector on Windows. That combination is the expensive part — race mode is several times slower, and Windows runners are the slowest of the three. Unsharded, the Windows job would be roughly 35–45 minutes and the gating check on every PR. Windows coverage is not decorative here: Brain's session history shows real Windows-only failures being debugged as recently as Oct 8 (file locking, path semantics, daemon/XDG storage behave differently there), and the race detector only finds Windows-timing races if it runs on Windows.

**Do you need it?** My assessment:

- You need *some* split if you keep race-enabled Windows tests as a required check. Dropping the harness entirely means either a ~40-minute bottleneck job or giving up `-race` on Windows.
- You probably don't need **8** shards. At ~34 total minutes, 4 shards (~9m each) would keep the critical path around 12 minutes — still faster than the unsharded macOS job — and halve the Windows runner spin-up overhead (which bills at 2x on private repos).
- The genuinely heavyweight part is not the shard count but the verification machinery (root inventory, evidence hashes, coverage union, the Python verifier suite). That was ported wholesale from entire-graph PR #189. It exists for a real reason — naive matrix sharding can silently drop tests — but it's the piece I'd scrutinize if you want to simplify, not the sharding itself.

No — 8 is more than you need. The numbers:

- Your pipeline's real bottleneck is `test (macos-latest)` at **20 minutes**. The Windows shards finish in 3–7m each, so they sit idle waiting on macOS anyway. Any shard count whose slowest shard stays under ~20m costs you **zero** PR feedback time.
- Total Windows test execution is ~34 minutes. At 4 shards that's ~8–11m per shard; even allowing for imbalance, comfortably under the 20m macOS ceiling and the 35m job timeout.
- Each extra shard pays a fixed tax: checkout, setup-go, setup-python, artifact download (~1–2m per runner), and Windows minutes bill at 2x on private repos. Halving the count saves ~4 runner spin-ups per PR with no latency cost.

The change is one line: `shardCount` in `tools/ci-bench/windows-production/settings.json:3` (the workflow matrix is derived from the plan, so nothing else needs touching; `max-parallel: 8` in test.yml becomes harmlessly oversized).

Two caveats:

what is the downside of dropping to 4?

The downsides are modest, but they exist:

- **Slower Windows-failure feedback.** Worst shard goes from ~7m to probably ~10–15m (imbalance included). PR merge time doesn't change — macOS at 20m still gates — but if you're specifically iterating on a Windows-only failure, each attempt's signal arrives later.
- **Bigger retry units.** A flaky failure reruns its whole shard. At 4 shards a rerun re-executes twice as many tests.
- **Less headroom as the suite grows.** ~34m of execution today means 4 shards sit at ~9m average. If the suite doubles, your worst shard pushes past 20m and Windows becomes the pipeline's critical path, forcing you to revisit. 8 shards defers that day.
- **Imbalance bites harder.** The planner balances by root count, not runtime (weights file is empty). With 8 bins a mis-weighted slow root costs a few minutes; with 4 bins it concentrates more. The remedy — populating `historical-weights.json` from shard timings — is documented but is extra work nobody has done yet.

What does *not* change: race-detection quality (roots run as the same separate test-binary invocations either way, just distributed differently), the verifier's no-dropped-tests guarantee, and coverage aggregation.

Net: you're trading future headroom and retry granularity for ~4 fewer Windows runner spin-ups per PR. Both positions are defensible; 4 is the right call only if the runner cost or queue contention is actually bothering you. If the shards' cost is noise in your billing, the honest answer is that 8 isn't hurting anything either.

It's not macOS — it's `internal/cli`, the same suite the Windows shards exist for. Breakdown of the 20 minutes:

- The job runs `go test -race -covermode=atomic -coverpkg=./... ./...` over the whole repo. Of the 18.6 minutes of package time, **`internal/cli` is 17 minutes**; the other 15 packages combined are ~1.5 minutes.
- `internal/cli` has **3,169 top-level tests across 442 test files**, and only 52 files use `t.Parallel()` — so within the package they run essentially one at a time, under race detection (5–10x CPU overhead) plus whole-repo atomic coverage instrumentation. macOS runners are also GitHub's weakest hardware, which is why Ubuntu does the identical job in 11m.

Where the time concentrates:

- Two tests alone are ~6.5 minutes: `TestBrainManifestObservedShapesRoundTrip` (218s) and `TestDemoCleanupPreservesSignalExitAndStopsSandboxChild` (180s).
- A cluster of lock tests (`TestSemanticIndexLockFailsFast`, `TestBundleExportLockFailsFast`, …) each take exactly 10.0s — that suspicious precision means they're waiting out a real timeout constant rather than doing 10s of work. There are several of these, and "fails fast" tests spending 10 wall-clock seconds each is the opposite of their name.
- A long tail of ~3,100 small tests doing real CLI integration work (spawned processes, SQLite, file I/O) that race mode makes slow.

So the honest picture: the Windows sharding harness treats the symptom, and macOS now exhibits the same disease untreated. The higher-leverage fixes are in the suite itself — shrink or split the two giant tests, inject a short timeout into the lock tests, and add `t.Parallel()` where tests are already isolated (the pinned `TestMain` gives each process fresh XDG storage, so many may already be safe). That would speed up every lane — macOS, Ubuntu, and all 8 Windows shards — instead of sharding a second platform.

# Review PR

Review a pull request with structured, actionable feedback.

## Arguments

- `` — PR number, URL, or branch name. If empty, review the current branch's open PR.

## Process

### 1. Fetch PR context

```
gh pr view <pr> --json title,body,baseRefName,headRefName,additions,deletions,changedFiles,commits,author
gh pr diff <pr>
```

Read the PR description carefully — it defines scope and intent. Everything you review should be evaluated against what the PR is trying to accomplish.

### 2. Understand the change

Before reviewing line-by-line:
- What is this PR doing and why?
- What files are touched and what's the blast radius?
- Are there any architectural implications?

### 3. Review with this checklist

**Correctness**
- Does the code do what the PR description says?
- Are there logic errors, off-by-one bugs, or unhandled edge cases?
- Are error paths handled correctly?

**Security**
- Any injection risks (SQL, XSS, command injection)?
- Are secrets, tokens, or credentials handled safely?
- Are inputs validated at system boundaries?

**Testing**
- Are there tests for the new/changed behavior?
- Do tests cover edge cases, not just the happy path?
- Are test assertions meaningful (not just "doesn't throw")?

**Design**
- Does the change follow existing codebase patterns and conventions?
- Is the abstraction level appropriate (not over/under-engineered)?
- Are there unnecessary changes outside the stated scope?

**Performance**
- Any N+1 queries, unbounded loops, or missing pagination?
- Are there opportunities for batching or caching that were missed?
- Will this scale with the data sizes it will encounter?

**Readability**
- Are names clear and consistent with the codebase?
- Is complex logic adequately explained?
- Would a future reader understand the "why" behind non-obvious decisions?

### 4. Adversarial review

Take a second, adversarial pass over the diff. Actively try to break the change — assume it has flaws and hunt for them across:

- **Performance** — worst-case inputs, hot paths, allocations, contention.
- **Stability** — race conditions, partial failures, retries, resource leaks, crash recovery.
- **Correctness** — inputs and states that violate the author's assumptions.
- **Simplicity** — code that could be deleted or replaced with something simpler/stdlib.
- **Platform design standards** — deviations from the platform's established design patterns and conventions.

Add any findings to the output using the same severity format.

### 5. Run /simplify

Run the `/simplify` skill (via the Skill tool) against the changed code and fold its findings into the review output.

### 6. Structure your output

For each finding, use this format:

**[severity] file:line — short title**
Description of the issue and why it matters. Include a suggested fix when possible.

Severity levels:
- **[blocking]** — Must fix before merge. Correctness bugs, security issues, data loss risks.
- **[important]** — Should fix. Design problems, missing tests for critical paths, performance issues.
- **[nit]** — Nice to fix. Style, naming, minor improvements. Don't block merge on these.
- **[question]** — Not necessarily wrong, but needs clarification or discussion.

### 7. Summary

End with a brief summary:
- Overall assessment (approve / request changes / needs discussion)
- What the PR does well
- Top 1-3 items that need attention
- Any scope concerns (changes that seem unrelated to the stated goal)

## Guidelines

- Review what's in the diff, not what you wish was there. Don't request unrelated refactoring.
- If the PR is large, focus on the most impactful files first.
- Be specific — "this could be better" is not useful. Show what "better" looks like.
- Distinguish between "this is wrong" and "I would do this differently." Only the former is blocking.
- If you're unsure about something, use [question] severity instead of asserting it's wrong.
- Read relevant source files (not just the diff) when you need context about how changed code integrates with the rest of the system.

## Review: trail 288 / `test-shards-pr-371`

**[important] brain_manifest_read_test.go:33 — case *name* was load-bearing control flow, and nothing enforced the fixture-above-cap invariant.** Renaming `"larger-than-default-read-limit"` would have silently disabled the override, leaving a 24 MiB fixture under the real 64 MiB cap — the test would keep passing while guarding nothing. **Fixed:** the lowered cap is now a `readCap` table field next to the sizes it must stay consistent with, and the subtest fails loudly if the fixture doesn't exceed it.

**[important] privacy_verification_regression_test.go:129 — restore wrote a literal, not the saved value, and duplicated the new pin test.** `2_000_000` appeared three times across two files; the cleanup would have silently "repaired" a changed production default instead of restoring it. **Fixed:** standard `prev`/restore idiom; the pin test alone owns the default. Ceiling also dropped 10,000 → 16 rows (identical LIMIT-plus-count path).

**[important] semantic_test.go — the lock-timeout override was an unenforced pairing.** Every contention test had to remember to call `shortSemanticLockTimeout` after `writeSemanticTestLock`; the next one written would silently wait the full 10s again. **Fixed:** folded into `writeSemanticTestLock` itself.

**[nit] demo_scripts_test.go — reinvented wait-delay literal.** The package already has `commandWaitDelay` (runner.go:73) documented for exactly this grandchild-inherits-the-pipe case. **Fixed**, which also dropped the added `time` import.

**[nit] safe_read.go — rationale comment written three times.** **Fixed:** one `var` group, one shared comment pointing at the pin test.

**[efficiency] fixtures still oversized for what they assert.** Stress manifest 24→5 MiB against a 4 MiB cap, unknown-fields 2 MiB→128 KiB, stdin test now uses the seam it sits beside (16 MiB→2 MiB of pipe traffic, with the chunk count snapshotted so the abandoned writer can't race the restore). Stress case: 20.2s → 3.1s.

**[question] demo test — latent CI verification gap (pre-existing, not fixed).** The old 3×60s pass pattern is only consistent with `sandbox_processes`' `ps` matcher finding nothing on CI runners: no kill attempted, directory still removed, orphan holding the pipe. If so, the "stops sandbox child" property has never actually been verified on CI. `WaitDelay` makes this cheap instead of hiding it, but a follow-up asserting the recorded child PID dies would close it properly.

**Skipped deliberately:** a generic `setForTest[T]` helper (against the package's 9 pre-existing inline prev/restore sites) and any shrinking of the observed-shape or 50k-commit incident fixtures (production-scale anchors).

**Why it's slow where it is:**

Your own laptop runs the identical suite in 6.3 minutes; the runner takes ~12.5 because it has a third of the cores and slower I/O. It's also GitHub's most expensive runner: macOS minutes bill at **10x Linux** on private repos.
- The suite compounds it: race detector + atomic whole-repo coverage, and `internal/cli` runs as one mostly-serial test binary, so extra cores beyond ~3 wouldn't help much today anyway.

**Your options, ranked by effort-to-payoff:**

1. **Depot macOS runners** — closest to a free lunch. Not one line — it's about **20 `runs-on` lines across 3 workflows, plus one-time setup**. Still an afternoon, not a project:

- **One-time:** install the Depot GitHub app on the org, create the Depot org/project, set up billing. No secrets or code changes — their runners register as self-hosted-style labels.
- **The mechanical part:** 20 `runs-on` edits (`ubuntu-latest` → `depot-ubuntu-latest`, `windows-latest` → `depot-windows-2022`, `macos-latest` → their macOS label). 17 are in `test.yml`, the rest in `release.yml`/`nightly.yml`, which aren't PR-gating and can move later or never.

Works as-is meanwhile. Depot's images track GitHub's runner images, so `setup-go`, `setup-python`, Playwright, and the actions cache all work unchanged.
